suggested a parametric model, introduced the concept of initial uncut 
chip geometry (iUCG), and developed a rapid feed planning strategy 
based on chip boundary and unchipped thickness distribution. 2.2.4. Cutting heat
In gear skiving, cutting heat is a crucial factor in tool life, workpiece 
surface quality, and the overall stability of the machining process. Schulze et al. [12] validated the correlation of the temperature distri­
bution in the developed 3D-FEM model by comparing simulated UCG, 
cutting force, and temperature data with experimental results under 
various process parameters. The experiments were carried out on a 
modified vertical turning machine tool made by INDEX Company. Wu 
et al. [41] developed a theoretical model for calculating cutting tem­
perature, which comprehensively accounts for cutting speed, cutting 
force, and tool-chip contact characteristics. Finally, this model is suc­
cessfully applied to the experiment of cutting an internal circular spur 
gear with an equal-rake angle arc-tooth slice cutter. The experimental 
device is shown in Fig. 7(a). Building on the work of [20,41], Zhang et al. [42] proposed a dy­
namic method based on digital twins for the skiving process. This 
approach used principal component analysis and extreme learning ma­
chines to streamline the coupled model, effectively leveraging skiving 
data for training. It established a correlation between cutting parame­
ters, cutting force, and cutting temperature, facilitating dynamic pre­
diction. Fig. 7(b) validates the accuracy of the predictions. Wen et al. 
[43] further improved the mathematical model for predicting cutting 
temperature. They looked at how different cutting parameters affected it 
and used genetic algorithm analysis to find the best combinations of 
parameters for different working conditions. Ren et al. [44] proposed a parametric modeling approach to calcu­
late the UCG and successfully predicted crater wear using the derived 
stress and temperature data. The results of UCG cutting characteristics 
are shown in Fig. 7(c) by AdvantEdge™ (Third Wave). They further 
studied the influence of the rake angle on the gear skiving process. The 
result shows that increasing the rake angle can improve the cutting 
performance, reduce the cutting temperature, and reduce the tool wear 
rate in some materials and suitable rake angle ranges [45]. These studies 
not only explore the mechanism of influencing cutting temperature but 
also provide a scientific basis for parameter selection and optimization 
in actual production. In this section, scholars have focused on key factors, such as cutting 
motion, cutting force, chips, and cutting temperature. These studies 
indicate that the development trend of gear skiving simulation has 
shifted from simple geometric modeling to complex physical process 
simulations. However, most studies primarily focus on the calculation of 
cutting force or exploring the relationship between chips, cutting heat, 
and cutting parameters. Few studies integrate these factors to system­
atically analyze their combined impact on workpiece machining quality 
and tool wear from a multidimensional perspective, as illustrated in 
Fig. 7(d). Future research should pay more attention to the key role of 
cutting temperature in gear skiving and deeply explore the coupling 
mechanism of cutting force, chip formation, and tool wear. 2.3.

items.question: Was ist die Ursache für Tooth-Shear-Fraß in Gears, und wie wird er durch eine einzelne extreme Belastung verursacht?
items.chunk_text:
ISO/TR 10825-2:2022(E)
—	 bearing failures or supports not parallel;
—	 distortion of the gearbox housing or foundation due to applied stresses or thermal effects;
—	 distortion of the gear teeth due to transmitted loads, centrifugal stresses or thermal effects;
—	 excessive radial space in the bearings, particularly those which do not have rolling elements;
—	 excessive internal clearance in rolling-element bearings;
—	 excessive tapered roller bearing endplay. Misalignment is always detrimental; proper alignment during operation is very important. 7.4	 Tooth shear fracture
Tooth shear is almost always caused by a single severe overload. 8	 Plastic Deformation
8.1	 General
Plastic deformation is permanent deformation that remains after removal of the applied load. It occurs 
when the stress exceeds the yield strength of the material. It can occur at the surface or subsurface of 
the active flanks of the gear teeth due to high contact stress, or at the root fillets of the gear teeth or the 
rim due to high bending stress (see 8.7). High contact stress can result from large loads or gear tooth 
impact (see 8.9) caused by vibration. 8.2	 Indentation
The active flanks of gear teeth can be damaged by indentations caused by foreign material that becomes 
trapped between mating teeth. Depending on the number, size and severity of the indentations, 
the damage can initiate other types of damage or failure. If plastic deformation associated with the 
indentations causes raised areas on the tooth active flank surface, it creates stress concentrations 
that can lead to subsequent contact fatigue. For gear teeth subjected to contact stresses greater than 
roughly 1,8 times the tensile yield strength of the material, local, subsurface yielding can occur. The 
subsurface plastic deformation causes grooves (see 8.3) on the surfaces of the active flanks of the teeth 
corresponding to the lines of contact between the mating gear teeth. 8.3	 Brinelling
True brinelling can occur on gear tooth flanks, typically when they are not rotating and are subjected 
to a sudden high impact load. With brinelling, usually the original grinding marks are visible 
microscopically in the bottoms of the dents. There is no relation between brinelling and false brinelling 
(5.7.2). 8.4 Cold flow
Cold flow is plastic deformation that occurs on the flank in the direction of sliding at a temperature 
lower than the recrystallization temperature. For steel, the recrystallization temperature usually 
ranges from around 450 °C to 900 °C, depending on severity of plastic deformation, grain size prior to 
plastic deformation, temperature at which plastic deformation occurs, time for which the plastically 
deformed metal is heated to attain recrystallization, and presence of dissolved or undissolved elements 
(see Reference [48]). It can occur with insufficient lubrication.

items.question: Was ist die Ursache für das Erschöpfen von Flüssigkeiten in der Nähe von Zahnreifen, was zu einer lokalen Druckveränderung und anschließender Kavitation führt?
items.chunk_text:
ISO/TR 10825-2:2022(E)
that nucleates vapor-filled bubbles within the liquid. When the bubbles travel into a region of higher 
pressure, they collapse as they change state from gas to liquid. The implosion of the bubbles transmits 
localized forces to the surface and can cause plastic deformation, work hardening and ductile fracture 
of the surface asperities. To the unaided eye, the gear tooth surface appears to be rough and clean as if 
it were sand blasted. 10.3	Erosion
Erosion can occur with clean fluids, but damage is much worse when there are solid contaminants in 
the fluid. See ISO 10825-1. 10.4	Electric discharge
10.4.1	 General
Gear teeth can be damaged if an electric current passes through the gear mesh (see Reference [55]). Electric currents can result from faulty insulation, induction effects or improper grounding. The 
electric discharge damage is caused by an electric arc discharge across the oil film between the active 
flanks of the mating gear teeth. The electric current can originate from many sources, including:
—	 electric motors;
—	 electric clutches or instrumentation;
—	 accumulation of static charge and subsequent discharge;
—	 during electric welding on or near the gear unit if the path to ground is not properly made around 
the gears rather than through them;
—	 during lightning strikes. An electric arc discharge across the oil film between mating gear teeth produces temperatures that 
can be high enough to locally melt the gear tooth surface. In some cases, it is difficult to detect with the 
unaided eye, but it can appear as an arc burn similar to a spot weld. Microscopically, the damage appears 
as small, hemispherical craters. The edges of the craters are smooth, and they can be surrounded by 
rounded particles that were once molten. SEM is often used to confirm electrical discharge damage. A metallurgical section taken transversely through the craters and acid etched can reveal austenitized 
and rehardened areas in white, bordered by tempered areas in black. Sometimes very small cracks 
are found near the craters. The damage to the gear teeth is proportional to the number and size of 
the points of arcing. Depending on its extent, electric discharge damage can be destructive to the gear 
teeth. If electric discharge damage is found on the gears, all associated bearings are usually examined since 
they often have similar damage. This can confirm that the damage is caused by electrical discharge, just 
as discovery of electrical discharge damage on bearing can lead to a check of the gears. See References 
[54] and [55]. 10.4.2	 Summary of methods that have been observed to reduce the risk of electrical discharge 
damage
The following methods can be considered for reducing the risk of electrical discharge damage:
—	 providing adequate electrical insulation;
—	 providing adequate grounding;
—	 ensuring proper welding grounding procedures are used.

et al. [60] designed a skiving tool for processing involute helical gears. Due to the existence of a top rake angle on the rake face, the gear pro­
cessed by the tool would have tooth profile errors. To address this, they 
proposed a correction method by adjusting the tool’s pressure angle. Additionally, Guo et al. [78] analyzed the theoretical tooth profile error 
of traditional skiving gears and how the rake angle of the skiving tool 
affected this error. Their study identified the primary error sources as 
the inherent tool error and the longitudinal deviation of the cutting 
edge. Han et al. [79] proposed a power-skiving profile correction 
method based on the reverse complement of involute tooth profile er­
rors. They also established the mathematical model of the involute tool, 
including rake and clearance angles. In terms of machining face gears, Xu et al. [80] introduced a profile 
modification method based on the skiving mathematical model for face 
gear pairs. By adjusting the tooth profile to optimize tooth contact and 
reduce stress concentration, this method significantly enhances the 
bearing capacity of the face gear. Han et al. [81] introduced a technol­
ogy for modifying the tooth surface on a six-axis machine tool. This 
technology adjusts the feed motion to optimize the meshing perfor­
mance of the non-orthogonal face gear, thereby achieving a tooth sur­
face with minimal transmission error. Le et al. [82] utilized the 
Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm to establish a mathematical model for 
closed-loop optimization technology. This model enables the modifica­
tion of flexible coefficients of the rack profile and machining-axis 
movement in accordance with the target tooth surface, thereby 
enhancing the tooth surface accuracy of power skiving helical face gears. Mo et al. [67] further advanced the skiving machining principle for face 
gears, proposing a corresponding tool design methodology and 
analyzing the effects of tool profile and installation errors on face gear 
tooth surface deviations. Guo et al. [83] investigated the impact of 
cutting depth, face gear rotation angle, and tool offset distance on de­
viations in the surface of face gear teeth. They used Vericut to validate 
their simulation of the machining process. These studies make it possible 
to accurately predict and correct tooth profile errors on machined gear 
surfaces from a theoretical perspective. From the perspective of machining motion, Guo et al. [84] developed 
a mathematical model for the conjugate cutting edges of skiving tool 
surfaces and proposed a tool path algorithm that adjusts the shaft angle 
to address the issue of tooth surface twists. Luu et al. [85] introduced a 
novel method for fabricating gears with variable pressure angles and 
spiral angles using a single tool. This method integrates the modification 
of tool geometry with the adjustment of CNC machine tool motion, 
enabling the generation of the target tooth surface shape through a dual 
closed-loop control system. By optimizing tool parameters, the surface quality of the workpiece 
can be effectively enhanced.

Figure 13. Tool paths after multipass machining of gear with longitudinal tooth modiﬁcation. Figure 14. Image of tooth surface stereometry with longitudinal modiﬁcation machined using the
multipass method (barrel tooth). Gears with straight tooth line are sensitive to misalignment errors of the shafts of the
cooperating gears. This problem can be eliminated by its longitudinal modiﬁcation. For
example, by programming the movement of the cutter, you can obtain gears with a slight
longitudinal modiﬁcation, including a version with two convex sides of the tooth (Cv-Cv)
and a version with one side of the tooth convex and the other concave (Cv-Cc). 5. Discussion
Gear machining is still carried out by specialized companies. The technology is
implemented in several stages. In the ﬁrst stage, all technological procedures are performed
from appropriately selected semiﬁnished material to produce a blank part. This process
is carried out on universal machine tools using available tools of a typical design. At this
point, the tolerance of the machining bases for the implementation of further technological
processes is important. Gear machining is carried out as roughing and ﬁnishing. During
rough machining, gear teeth are cut on the shell using various methods depending on the
dimensions and type of gear. The production of gear teeth is carried out on specialized
machines that are dedicated only to this purpose using specialized tools. The next stage is
ﬁnishing, which is carried out immediately after rough machining if the machined wheel is
to be in a soft condition or after heat or thermochemical treatment. The process of machining the entire gear wheel is complicated and requires several
specialized and universal machine tools and special tools designed for a speciﬁc technology. There is lack of ﬂexibility in terms of quick response to customer requirements. Switching
from the production of one type of gear to another requires the manufacturer to incur high
costs for the purchase of machines and tools, which also extends the order time.

To 
ensure a comprehensive and in-depth review of gear skiving technology, 
this paper conducted a systematic literature search across multiple 
authoritative academic databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, 
Google Scholar, Engineering Village, and IEEE Xplore. The search pri­
marily focused on “Power Skiving,” “Scudding,” “Gear Skiving,” 
“Slicing,” and “Super Skiving System.” A keyword search method was 
used to find specific terms like “cutting force,” “uncut chip geometry,” 
“cutting temperature,” “simulation,” “machining parameters,” “tool 
design,” “tool manufacturing,” “tool errors,” “tool life,” and “tool wear.” 
To make sure that all research content that was closely related to gear 
skiving technology was found, Boolean operators like “AND” and “OR” 
were used to narrow the search. Ultimately, 110 high-quality articles 
were selected based on thematic relevance, academic influence, and 
research quality. These studies provide a solid theoretical foundation for 
this review and contribute to a perspective on the current advancements 
in gear skiving technology. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 pro­
vides a detailed summary of the key research areas in gear skiving 
technology, including machining principle, covering the fundamental 
cutting mechanisms; cutting process simulation and mathematical 
modeling, which are used to analyze and simulate the gear skiving 
process; influence of parameters on the process, discussing the effects of 
various parameters on machining performance; tool design, focusing on 
the development of more efficient and durable skiving tools; error 
analysis and correction, analyzes the error source and its influence on 
machining accuracy; tool manufacturing, exploring how grinding tech­
niques can enhance tool performance; tool life and wear, discusses the 
factors affecting tool life and wear and the necessity of developing wear 
monitoring system. Finally, Section 3 discusses the current practical

Figure 12 — Hydrogen pressure buildup during rapid cooling (see Reference [53])
9.4.2 
Hydrogen flake term
Under the pressure of hydrogen, steel splits and forms so-called “flakes” or “breaking points” that look 
like “snowflakes”. This generally only occurs in low strength steels. The term “flakes” refers to defects that appear as easily identifiable shiny cups on the broken surfaces 
of the parts. They correspond to areas where hydrogen has recombined into molecular form. See 
Figure 13. Figure 13 — Fracture caused by hydrogen flake, with enlarged view of area with flake
The defect can occur prior to loading, and the damage is irreversible. This type of damage, which affects low forging ratio or no forging ratio steels, has become relatively 
rare. In this case, low-carbon content steels are much less sensitive than hard steels (limited to 0,3 % C).
